claim: Lattice light sheet microscopy offers a unique combination of three-dimensional imaging with high spatial and temporal resolution and low phototoxicity.
source: To address these issues, we employed the recently developed lattice light sheet microscope (Chen et al., 2014), which offers a unique combination of three-dimensional imaging with high spatial and temporal resolution and low phototoxicity.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2014, which describes the lattice light sheet microscope technology.

claim: The utrophin-based actin probe binds preferentially to cortical actin surrounding the cell body and is largely excluded from the more dynamic, branched actin networks that drive pseudopod extension.
source: Therefore, we chose the utrophin-based actin probe, which binds preferentially to cortical actin surrounding the cell body and is largely excluded from the more dynamic, branched actin networks that drive pseudopod extension (Belin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Belin et al., 2014, which characterizes the binding properties of the utrophin-based actin probe.

claim: No actin probe binds exclusively to the dynamic, branched actin networks of the pseudopod, including the widely used probe, Lifeact.
source: No actin probe binds exclusively to the dynamic, branched actin networks of the pseudopod, including the widely used probe, Lifeact (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which shows that Lifeact does not exclusively label dynamic pseudopod actin networks.

claim: HL-60 cells build pseudopods that are filled with polymerized actin, easily visualized in fixed cells using phalloidin.
source: Neutrophil-like HL-60 cells build pseudopods that are filled with polymerized actin, easily visualized in fixed cells using phalloidin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, which show phalloidin staining of actin in pseudopods.

claim: Three-dimensional pseudopods turn out to be composed of thin (<0.75 µm), flat sheets that sometimes interleave to form rosettes.
source: Surprisingly, three-dimensional pseudopods turn out to be composed of thin (<0.75 µm), flat sheets that sometimes interleave to form rosettes.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from lattice light sheet microscopy data presented throughout the manuscript, including measurements of pseudopod thickness.

claim: The laminar nature of pseudopods is not templated by an external surface, but likely reflects a linear arrangement of regulatory molecules.
source: Their laminar nature is not templated by an external surface, but likely reflects a linear arrangement of regulatory molecules.
evidence: The claim is based on observations that pseudopods maintain lamellar morphology in 3D collagen matrices and inference about the underlying molecular organization.

claim: Arp2/3-dependent pseudopods are dispensable for three-dimensional locomotion.
source: Although we find that Arp2/3-dependent pseudopods are dispensable for three-dimensional locomotion, their elimination dramatically decreases the frequency of cell turning, and pseudopod dynamics increase when cells change direction, highlighting the important role pseudopods play in pathfinding.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that cells treated with CK-666 (Arp2/3 inhibitor) can still migrate through collagen matrices.

claim: Elimination of Arp2/3-dependent pseudopods dramatically decreases the frequency of cell turning.
source: Although we find that Arp2/3-dependent pseudopods are dispensable for three-dimensional locomotion, their elimination dramatically decreases the frequency of cell turning, and pseudopod dynamics increase when cells change direction, highlighting the important role pseudopods play in pathfinding.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cell turning behavior in control versus CK-666 treated cells shown in Figure 6.

claim: Pseudopod dynamics increase when cells change direction.
source: Although we find that Arp2/3-dependent pseudopods are dispensable for three-dimensional locomotion, their elimination dramatically decreases the frequency of cell turning, and pseudopod dynamics increase when cells change direction, highlighting the important role pseudopods play in pathfinding.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing correlation between pseudopod formation and cell turning events, as visualized in Figure 6B.

claim: Movement of leading-edge lamellipodia is driven by growth of branched actin networks nucleated and crosslinked by the Arp2/3 complex.
source: Previous work, mainly on fibroblasts and epithelial cells, has established that movement of leading-edge lamellipodia is driven by growth of branched actin networks nucleated and crosslinked by the Arp2/3 complex.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge from previous work on fibroblasts and epithelial cells.

claim: Adhesion-based cell migration is restricted to the animal lineage.
source: This mode of cell migration appears to be restricted to the animal lineage, where it relies on the presence of specific ligands in the extracellular environment and plays essential roles in embryonic development, wound healing, and tissue homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the phylogenetic distribution of adhesion-based migration.

claim: A more widely dispersed form of cell crawling was probably present in the last common ancestor of all eukaryotes.
source: A more widely dispersed form of cell crawling—probably present in the last common ancestor of all eukaryotes (Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017)—requires only weak, non-specific interaction with the extracellular environment and can achieve speeds several orders of magnitude faster than adhesion-based movement (Loomis et al., 2012; Preston and King, 1978; Lämmermann et al., 2008; Buenemann et al., 2010; Butler et al., 2010; Loomis et al., 2012; Petrie and Yamada, 2015; Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017, which discusses the evolutionary origins of cell crawling.

claim: Fast, weakly adherent cell crawling can achieve speeds several orders of magnitude faster than adhesion-based movement.
source: A more widely dispersed form of cell crawling—probably present in the last common ancestor of all eukaryotes (Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017)—requires only weak, non-specific interaction with the extracellular environment and can achieve speeds several orders of magnitude faster than adhesion-based movement (Loomis et al., 2012; Preston and King, 1978; Lämmermann et al., 2008; Buenemann et al., 2010; Butler et al., 2010; Loomis et al., 2012; Petrie and Yamada, 2015; Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the speed differences between adhesion-based and adhesion-independent migration.

claim: Disrupting pseudopod formation can increase the speed and persistence of migration.
source: These three-dimensional pseudopods may contribute to forward motion of crawling and swimming cells (Van Haastert, 2011), but recent work has revealed that disrupting pseudopod formation can increase the speed and persistence of migration (Leithner et al., 2016; Vargas et al., 2016), implying that complex pseudopods might be more important for exploring the external environment than for driving forward motion.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Leithner et al., 2016 and Vargas et al., 2016, which report increased migration speed upon pseudopod disruption.

claim: Complex pseudopods might be more important for exploring the external environment than for driving forward motion.
source: These three-dimensional pseudopods may contribute to forward motion of crawling and swimming cells (Van Haastert, 2011), but recent work has revealed that disrupting pseudopod formation can increase the speed and persistence of migration (Leithner et al., 2016; Vargas et al., 2016), implying that complex pseudopods might be more important for exploring the external environment than for driving forward motion.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on observations that disrupting pseudopods increases migration speed, suggesting their primary role is not propulsion.

claim: The spatial resolution of lattice light sheet microscopy data was approximately 230 nm in XY and 370 nm in Z.
source: The spatial resolution of the resulting data was approximately 230 nm in XY and 370 nm in Z (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2014, which characterizes the resolution of the lattice light sheet microscope.

claim: Lamellar pseudopods have a thickness between 430 and 800 nm.
source: Given the resolution of lattice light sheet microscopy (~230 nm in XY [Chen et al., 2014]), we estimate that the actual thickness of lamellar pseudopods lies between 430 and 800 nm.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from multiple imaging modalities including lattice light sheet microscopy, confocal microscopy, and scanning electron microscopy.

claim: Cells crawling across coverslips and those crawling through collagen networks build sheets with similar flatness.
source: Cells crawling across coverslips, as well as those crawling through collagen networks, build sheets with similar flatness (Figure 2D), raising the question of how cells can form flat structures without the surface template mechanism proposed for the assembly of flat lamellipodia of adherent cells (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of pseudopod flatness shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Both sheet and rosette pseudopods largely excluded utrophin-based actin probes.
source: Firstly, both sheet and rosette pseudopods largely excluded utrophin-based actin probes (Figure 1B) and both types of protrusion disappeared in the presence of CK-666 (Figure 4B, Video 11, and Video 12), a small-molecule inhibitor of the Arp2/3 complex (Nolen et al., 2009), arguing that sheets and rosettes are formed by rapidly assembling, branched actin networks.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating exclusion of utrophin probe from pseudopods.

claim: Both sheet and rosette pseudopods disappeared in the presence of CK-666, a small-molecule inhibitor of the Arp2/3 complex.
source: Firstly, both sheet and rosette pseudopods largely excluded utrophin-based actin probes (Figure 1B) and both types of protrusion disappeared in the presence of CK-666 (Figure 4B, Video 11, and Video 12), a small-molecule inhibitor of the Arp2/3 complex (Nolen et al., 2009), arguing that sheets and rosettes are formed by rapidly assembling, branched actin networks.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing loss of pseudopods upon CK-666 treatment, shown in Figure 4B and Videos 11-12.

claim: Sheets and rosettes are formed by rapidly assembling, branched actin networks.
source: Firstly, both sheet and rosette pseudopods largely excluded utrophin-based actin probes (Figure 1B) and both types of protrusion disappeared in the presence of CK-666 (Figure 4B, Video 11, and Video 12), a small-molecule inhibitor of the Arp2/3 complex (Nolen et al., 2009), arguing that sheets and rosettes are formed by rapidly assembling, branched actin networks.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that pseudopods are sensitive to Arp2/3 inhibition, which is known to disrupt branched actin network assembly.

claim: Lamellae within rosettes have the same thickness (690 ± 20 nm, n = 18) as the simple lamellar pseudopods.
source: Secondly, lamellae within rosettes have the same thickness (690 ± 20 nm, n = 18, Figure 3B) as the simple lamellar pseudopods.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3B comparing thickness of sheets and rosette petals.

claim: In a uniform field of chemoattractant, pseudopodial sheets and rosettes both have a lifespan of approximately 60 s.
source: Fourthly, in a uniform field of chemoattractant, pseudopodial sheets and rosettes both have a lifespan of approximately 60 s, from initial appearance to final disappearance (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of pseudopod duration shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Protrusion lifespan does not depend on external mechanical support.
source: This lifetime remains similar whether cells are migrating across flat surfaces or through collagen networks (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), indicating that protrusion lifespan does not depend on external mechanical support.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that pseudopod lifespans are similar in 2D and 3D environments, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Approximately 75% of both sheet and rosette pseudopods disappear by collapsing into a tangle of linear structures that resemble filopodia.
source: Finally, approximately 75% of both sheet and rosette pseudopods disappear in an identical manner, by collapsing into a tangle of linear structures that resemble filopodia (Figure 3E (rosette) and Video 1 (sheet), see also Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 3E, Video 1, and Figure 4A.

claim: Lamellar pseudopods first appeared as linear deformations running across the surface of the plasma membrane.
source: The lamellar elements that form pseudopods—both sheets and rosettes—first appeared as linear deformations running across the surface of the plasma membrane (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is based on observations from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Nascent pseudopods grow at a characteristic rate of 11.9 ± 5.4 µm/min.
source: These low 'ridges' formed mature pseudopods by growing rapidly away from the cell body, at a characteristic rate of 11.9 ± 5.4 µm/min (n = 4).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative measurements of pseudopod growth rates from time-lapse imaging data.

claim: As each nascent protrusion grew, its distal edge remained linear, leaving a flat pseudopod in its wake.
source: Remarkably, as each nascent protrusion grew, its distal edge remained linear, leaving a flat pseudopod in its wake.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from time-lapse imaging of pseudopod formation.

claim: The WAVE regulatory complex forms a series of thin arcs, or 'waves,' that originate somewhere in the cell body and then advance outward along the cell's ventral surface when imaged by TIRF microscopy.
source: A previous study (Weiner et al., 2007) employed TIRF microscopy to image localization and dynamics of the WAVE regulatory complex in HL-60 cells crawling on glass coverslips. When imaged in the region proximal (within ~100 nm) to the coverslip, the WAVE regulatory complex forms a series of thin arcs, or 'waves,' that originate somewhere in the cell body and then advance outward along the cell's ventral surface.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Weiner et al., 2007, which describes WAVE complex dynamics in HL-60 cells.

claim: Each outward-moving wave is actually the edge of an individual sheet pressed into the TIRF plane as it extends forward.
source: Our observation that the pseudopod of an HL-60 cell is composed of multiple lamellar sheets suggests that each outward-moving wave is actually the edge of an individual sheet pressed into the TIRF plane as it extends forward.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that pseudopods are lamellar and the known behavior of WAVE complex in TIRF microscopy.

claim: The cell's ventral surface is not smooth and does not make uniformly close contact with the fibronectin-coated coverslip to which it adheres.
source: RICM revealed that the cell's ventral surface is not smooth and does not make uniformly close contact with the fibronectin-coated coverslip to which it adheres, consistent with previous observations (Sullivan and Mandell, 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by RICM imaging data and citation to Sullivan and Mandell, 1983.

claim: The ventral surface forms dynamic and complex patterns of close contact, including lines that travel toward the front of the crawling cell.
source: Instead, the ventral surface forms dynamic and complex patterns of close contact, including lines that travel toward the front of the crawling cell (Figure 5, Video 13).
evidence: The claim is supported by RICM imaging data shown in Figure 5 and Video 13.

claim: There is enrichment of WAVE complex at moving lines of close contact between the cell and coverslip.
source: Consistent with our interpretation, we also see enrichment of WAVE complex at these moving lines of close contact (Figure 5, Video 13).
evidence: The claim is supported by simultaneous TIRF and RICM imaging shown in Figure 5 and Video 13.

claim: Inhibition of Arp2/3 complex activity decreases the volume of the largest pseudopod produced by crawling cells by an average of 40%.
source: This method of automated identification and quantification reveals that inhibition of Arp2/3 complex activity decreases the volume of the largest pseudopod produced by crawling cells by an average of 40% (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and Videos 14–15), a significant decrease despite the within-cell variability of pseudopod volume (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of pseudopod volumes in control versus CK-666 treated cells shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The rate of pseudopod formation decreased from 1.9 pseudopods/min to 0.8 pseudopods/min upon Arp2/3 inhibition.
source: Similarly, visual inspection of time-lapse sequences revealed that the rate of pseudopod formation decreased from 1.9 pseudopods/min to 0.8 pseudopods/min upon Arp2/3 inhibition (Control: n = 9 cells over 40.7 min; CK-666 treated: n = 7 cells over 22.1 min).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative analysis of pseudopod formation rates from time-lapse imaging of control and CK-666 treated cells.

claim: Cells treated with CK-666 retained the ability to migrate through collagen networks in a uniform field of chemoattractant.
source: Despite the loss of dynamic pseudopods, cells treated with CK-666 retained the ability to migrate through collagen networks in a uniform field of chemoattractant.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from time-lapse imaging of CK-666 treated cells showing continued migration.

claim: CK-666 treated cells moved more slowly (5.42 vs 8.57 um/min) than control cells.
source: The treated cells, however, moved more slowly (5.42 vs 8.57 um/min, Figure 6E) and appeared to travel along much straighter trajectories than control cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cell migration speeds shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Control cells changed direction 2 to 3 times more often than CK-666 treated cells.
source: According to both metrics, control cells changed direction 2 to 3 times more often than the CK-666 treated cells (method 1: 2.73 vs 1.15 turns/min, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B; method 2: 3.41 vs 1.09 turns/min, Figure 6D–F), and displayed greater turn activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cell turning behavior using two different methods, shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Control cell trajectories reveal frequent turns, each of which appears correlated with a dramatic increase in pseudopod dynamics.
source: Control cell trajectories reveal frequent turns, each of which appears correlated with a dramatic increase in pseudopod dynamics.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of cell trajectories overlaid with pseudopod dynamics data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: While control cells frequently build pseudopods in the direction of cell motion, the protrusions built by CK-666 treated cells are more uniformly distributed.
source: Furthermore, while control cells frequently build pseudopods in the direction of cell motion, the protrusions built by CK-666 treated cells are more uniformly distributed (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of pseudopod directionality shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Complex pseudopods formed by fast-moving HL-60 cells are actually composed of dynamic lamellar elements.
source: Lattice light sheet microscopy reveals that complex pseudopods formed by fast-moving HL-60 cells are actually composed of dynamic lamellar elements.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from lattice light sheet microscopy showing that pseudopods have lamellar structure.

claim: Some pseudopods are isolated, free-standing lamellae, while others are rosettes composed of multiple lamellar elements, often connected by T- and Y-shaped junctions.
source: Some pseudopods are isolated, free-standing lamellae, while others are rosettes composed of multiple lamellar elements, often connected by T- and Y-shaped junctions.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from lattice light sheet microscopy showing different pseudopod morphologies.

claim: The sheet-like morphology of lamellar building blocks does not depend on interaction with a flat surface.
source: These lamellar building blocks share common structural features, including a characteristic thickness, but their sheet-like morphology does not depend on interaction with a flat surface.
evidence: The claim is based on observations that pseudopods maintain lamellar morphology in 3D collagen matrices without surface contact.

claim: Similar lamellar and rosette protrusions have been identified in published scanning electron micrographs of several different cell types.
source: We identified similar lamellar and rosette protrusions in published scanning electron micrographs of several different cells types, including differentiated HL-60 cells (Fleck et al., 2005), Jurkat T cells (Nicholson-Dykstra and Higgs, 2008) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), human neutrophils migrating through a chemoattractant gradient (Zigmond and Sullivan, 1979), dendritic cells (Coates et al., 2003; Fisher et al., 2008; Felts et al., 2010), T-cells (Brown et al., 2003) and monocytes (Majstoravich et al., 2004) from human blood, as well as Dictyostelium amoebae (Gerisch et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies showing similar structures in different cell types.

claim: Fast-moving leukocytes can assemble free-standing lamellar pseudopods without the aid of a surface 'template.'
source: From our current work and previous observations, we propose two basic principles that define pseudopod morphology in these and other cells that build lamellar pseudopods. First, fast-moving leukocytes can assemble free-standing lamellar pseudopods without the aid of a surface 'template.'
evidence: The claim is based on observations that pseudopods maintain lamellar morphology in 3D environments without surface contact.

claim: More complex three-dimensional pseudopods can be resolved into lamellar components.
source: Second, more complex three-dimensional pseudopods can be resolved into lamellar components.
evidence: The claim is based on observations that rosette pseudopods are composed of multiple interleaved lamellar sheets.

claim: Free-standing pseudopodial sheets are thicker (~430–800 nm) than attached lamellipodia (<200 nm).
source: Although they resemble attached lamellipodia, the pseudopodial sheets we describe are thicker (~430–800 nm vs. <200 nm (Abercrombie et al., 1971)) and grow at faster rates (Ingram, 1969; Abercrombie et al., 1971).
evidence: The claim is based on measurements of pseudopod thickness compared to published measurements of lamellipodial thickness.

claim: Free-standing pseudopodial sheets grow at faster rates than attached lamellipodia.
source: Although they resemble attached lamellipodia, the pseudopodial sheets we describe are thicker (~430–800 nm vs. <200 nm (Abercrombie et al., 1971)) and grow at faster rates (Ingram, 1969; Abercrombie et al., 1971).
evidence: The claim is based on measurements of pseudopod growth rates compared to published rates for lamellipodia.

claim: In vitro, the morphology of a branched actin network is determined by the spatial arrangement of the regulatory molecules that activate the Arp2/3 complex.
source: Reconstitution of Arp2/3-dependent branched actin network assembly provides a simple explanation: in vitro, the morphology of a branched actin network is determined by the spatial arrangement of the regulatory molecules that activate the Arp2/3 complex.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from in vitro reconstitution experiments.

claim: One-dimensional arrangement of Arp2/3 activator along a thin glass fiber produces a flat, sheet-like actin network.
source: One-dimensional arrangement of Arp2/3 activator along a thin glass fiber, for example, produces a flat, sheet-like actin network (Achard et al., 2010; Hu and Kuhn, 2012), while a two-dimensional square of Arp2/3 activator produces a more three-dimensional rectangular solid (Bieling et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to in vitro reconstitution studies by Achard et al., 2010 and Hu and Kuhn, 2012.

claim: A two-dimensional square of Arp2/3 activator produces a more three-dimensional rectangular solid.
source: One-dimensional arrangement of Arp2/3 activator along a thin glass fiber, for example, produces a flat, sheet-like actin network (Achard et al., 2010; Hu and Kuhn, 2012), while a two-dimensional square of Arp2/3 activator produces a more three-dimensional rectangular solid (Bieling et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bieling et al., 2016, which describes in vitro reconstitution experiments.

claim: Once formed, a thin, flat actin network should remain stable as it grows.
source: Mathematical models of branched actin network formation agree with these reconstitution results and suggest that, once formed, a thin, flat actin network should remain stable as it grows (Schmeiser and Winkler, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schmeiser and Winkler, 2015, which presents mathematical modeling of actin network growth.

claim: The approximate dimensionality of nucleation and polymerase activity on the membrane is one less than the approximate dimensionality of the actin network generated by this activity.
source: Generalizing, we propose that the approximate dimensionality of nucleation and polymerase activity on the membrane is one less than the approximate dimensionality of the actin network (and protrusion) generated by this activity.
evidence: The claim is a generalization inferred from in vitro reconstitution experiments and mathematical models.

claim: A filopodium (dimension ~1) grows from a point source (dimension ~0) of nucleation/polymerase activity.
source: In other words, a filopodium (dimension ~1) grows from a point source (dimension ~0) of nucleation/polymerase activity while a lamellar pseudopod (dimension ~2) grows from a line source (dimension ~1).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the proposed relationship between nucleation dimensionality and protrusion dimensionality.

claim: A lamellar pseudopod (dimension ~2) grows from a line source (dimension ~1) of nucleation/polymerase activity.
source: In other words, a filopodium (dimension ~1) grows from a point source (dimension ~0) of nucleation/polymerase activity while a lamellar pseudopod (dimension ~2) grows from a line source (dimension ~1).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the proposed relationship between nucleation dimensionality and protrusion dimensionality.

claim: The two-dimensional nature of lamellar protrusions follows as a direct consequence of the one-dimensional organization of the Arp2/3 activation machinery.
source: We therefore propose that the two-dimensional nature of lamellar protrusions follows as a direct consequence of the one-dimensional organization of the Arp2/3 activation machinery (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from in vitro reconstitution experiments and observations of WAVE complex organization.

claim: Direct activators of Arp2/3 activity—WASP and the WAVE regulatory complex—form dynamic, linear arcs that propagate like traveling waves when observed at the cell surface by TIRF microscopy.
source: This model for the assembly of flat pseudopods is supported by previous observations that activators of Arp2/3-dependent actin assembly appear in linear patterns on the membrane. When observed at the cell surface by TIRF microscopy, direct activators of Arp2/3 activity—WASP and the WAVE regulatory complex—form dynamic, linear arcs that propagate like traveling waves (Weiner et al., 2007; Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Weiner et al., 2007 and Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017, which describe WAVE and WASP localization patterns.

claim: Only WASP and WAVE have been shown to form lines, while further upstream components of the activation cascade, such as Rac, exhibit more diffuse localization patterns.
source: To date, only these two Arp2/3 activators have been shown to form lines, while further upstream components of the activation cascade, such as Rac, exhibit more diffuse localization patterns (Weiner et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Weiner et al., 2007 and Yang et al., 2016, which describe localization patterns of different signaling molecules.

claim: Multiple dynamic Arp2/3 activation zones produce multiple lamellar pseudopods that can interact to form complex rosettes.
source: We propose that these multiple dynamic Arp2/3 activation zones produce multiple lamellar pseudopods that can interact to form complex rosettes.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on observations of WAVE complex localization and pseudopod morphology.

claim: Membrane-bound circles of WAVE complex initiate formation of cylindrical, cup-like protrusions during macropinocytosis in Dictyostelium cells.
source: Similarly, recent lattice light sheet microscopy of Dictyostelium cells revealed membrane-bound circles of WAVE complex (known as SCAR in Dictyostelium) initiating formation of cylindrical, cup-like protrusions during macropinocytosis (Veltman et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Veltman et al., 2016, which describes WAVE/SCAR localization during macropinocytosis.

claim: Cells that produce only a single, stable line of Arp2/3 activators at the leading edge produce only a single lamellar protrusion.
source: In contrast, cells that produce only a single, stable line of Arp2/3 activators at the leading edge (e.g. Drosophila S2 cells [Kunda et al., 2003] and epithelial cells [Gautier et al., 2011]) produce only a single lamellar protrusion.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kunda et al., 2003 and Gautier et al., 2011, which describe Arp2/3 activator localization in different cell types.

claim: Complex pseudopods are not required for HL-60 cell migration, but they do play a role in direction change.
source: We find that although complex pseudopods are not required for HL-60 cell migration, they do play a role in direction change.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data showing that CK-666 treated cells can migrate but turn less frequently.

claim: The size and number of membrane protrusions increase dramatically when cells change direction.
source: Using automated methods to detect and measure pseudopods we find that the size and number of these membrane protrusions increase dramatically when cells change direction and that blocking pseudopod formation reduces the frequency of direction changes (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6 correlating pseudopod dynamics with cell turning.

claim: Blocking pseudopod formation reduces the frequency of direction changes.
source: Using automated methods to detect and measure pseudopods we find that the size and number of these membrane protrusions increase dramatically when cells change direction and that blocking pseudopod formation reduces the frequency of direction changes (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced turning frequency in CK-666 treated cells, shown in Figure 6.

claim: Reducing WAVE activity in dendritic cells abolishes pseudopod formation, yet accelerates the crawling of cells in simple confined spaces.
source: These results provide a simple explanation for recent work from the Sixt lab, who found that reducing WAVE activity in dendritic cells abolishes pseudopod formation, yet accelerates the crawling of cells in simple confined spaces (Leithner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Leithner et al., 2016, which describes effects of WAVE inhibition on dendritic cell migration.

claim: Pseudopod-deficient dendritic cells fail to reorient in changing gradients of chemoattractant.
source: Interestingly, the pseudopod-deficient dendritic cells fail to reorient in changing gradients of chemoattractant, and migrate more slowly toward a chemotactic source within complex three-dimensional environments compared to control cells.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from Leithner et al., 2016, describing behavior of WAVE-inhibited dendritic cells.

claim: Arp2/3 activity at the front of migrating dendritic cells is responsible for speed-fluctuating behavior.
source: Similarly, in another recent paper, the Piel and Lennon-Dumenil labs found that Arp2/3 activity at the front of migrating dendritic cells was responsible for speed-fluctuating behavior (Vargas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vargas et al., 2016, which describes the role of Arp2/3 in dendritic cell migration dynamics.

claim: The three-dimensional pseudopods produced by fast-moving leukocytes promote the cell turning required for exploration of the local environment.
source: Together with these findings in dendritic cells, our results suggest that the three-dimensional pseudopods produced by fast-moving leukocytes promote the cell turning required for exploration of the local environment.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' data combined with findings from other studies on dendritic cells.

claim: A pseudopodial sheet is much thinner than a spherical bleb but can sweep out a comparable volume.
source: We speculate that broad, lamellar pseudopodia and extended rosettes may be uniquely adept structures for probing a cell's environment. A pseudopodial sheet is much thinner than a spherical bleb but can sweep out a comparable volume.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the functional advantages of lamellar pseudopods based on their geometric properties.

claim: Linear filopodia would have to move both back and forth and side to side to search the same volume as a lamellar sheet, and would provide limited surface contact.
source: Linear filopodia, in contrast, would have to move both back and forth and side to side to search the same volume, and would provide limited surface contact.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the relative efficiency of different protrusion types for environmental exploration.

claim: UCSF Chimera is a freely available, open-source software platform developed to render and analyze three-dimensional atomic structures and density maps.
source: UCSF Chimera is a freely available, open-source software platform developed to render and analyze three-dimensional atomic structures (Pettersen et al., 2004) and density maps (Goddard et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pettersen et al., 2004 and Goddard et al., 2007, which describe UCSF Chimera software.

claim: The loss of Arp2/3 activity dramatically reduced adhesion of HL-60 cells to fibronectin-coated coverslips.
source: This analysis was limited to cells moving through three-dimensional collagen matrices because we found that the loss of Arp2/3 activity dramatically reduced adhesion of HL-60 cells to fibronectin-coated coverslips.
evidence: The claim is based on observations that CK-666 treated cells did not adhere well to coverslips.

claim: While control cells built lamellar pseudopods, CK-666 treated cells formed long, tubular protrusions.
source: While control cells built lamellar pseudopods, CK-666 treated cells formed long, tubular protrusions (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B comparing control and CK-666 treated cells.

claim: The absence of fluorescent utrophin from membrane-proximal regions of the cell provides a convenient marker to identify protrusions driven by the growth of branched actin networks.
source: We used the absence of fluorescent utrophin from membrane-proximal regions of the cell as a convenient marker to identify protrusions driven by the growth of branched actin networks, and automated this process by subtracting the volume enclosed by a utrophin-based actin probe from the volume enclosed by the plasma membrane marker (Figure 6A, Video 14).
evidence: The claim describes the method developed by the authors for automated pseudopod detection, illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: Time-lapse sequences generated by the lattice light sheet microscope comprised two-color image stacks, collected through entire cell volumes at 1.3 s intervals with minimal photobleaching and no evidence of phototoxicity.
source: Time-lapse sequences generated by the lattice light sheet microscope comprised two-color image stacks, collected through entire cell volumes at 1.3 s intervals with minimal photobleaching and no evidence of phototoxicity.
evidence: The claim describes the technical capabilities of the lattice light sheet microscope used in the study.

claim: Lamellar pseudopods maintained an approximately constant thickness throughout their lifetime.
source: Despite being unsupported, these pseudopods maintained a lamellar morphology with an approximately constant thickness throughout their lifetime (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 2E tracking pseudopod thickness over time.

claim: Lamellar pseudopods have a similar profile whether cells crawl across glass or through a collagen matrix.
source: Regardless of whether cells crawled across glass or through a collagen matrix, their lamellar pseudopods shared several common features, including a similar profile (Figure 2C) and thickness (780 ± 137 nm standard deviation, n = 18 cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2C comparing pseudopods in different environments.

claim: Lamellar pseudopods have a thickness of 780 ± 137 nm (standard deviation, n = 18 cells) when measured from surface-rendered LLSm data.
source: Regardless of whether cells crawled across glass or through a collagen matrix, their lamellar pseudopods shared several common features, including a similar profile (Figure 2C) and thickness (780 ± 137 nm standard deviation, n = 18 cells).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative measurements of pseudopod thickness from lattice light sheet microscopy data.

claim: The thickness measured from surface-rendered LLSm data agrees with measurements made on other types of data, including raw lattice light sheet data (567 ± 64 nm on glass and 689 ± 86 nm in collagen).
source: The thickness measured from surface-rendered LLSm data agrees with measurements made on other types of data, including: raw lattice light sheet data (567 ± 64 nm on glass and 689 ± 86 nm in collagen); spinning disk confocal images of phalloidin-stained actin (505 ± 49 nm for a sheet and 533 ± 123 nm for a rosette petal); and scanning electron micrographs, which suggest a thickness of ~640 nm (Fleck et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from multiple imaging modalities, providing convergent evidence for pseudopod thickness.

claim: Spinning disk confocal images of phalloidin-stained actin show pseudopod thickness of 505 ± 49 nm for a sheet and 533 ± 123 nm for a rosette petal.
source: The thickness measured from surface-rendered LLSm data agrees with measurements made on other types of data, including: raw lattice light sheet data (567 ± 64 nm on glass and 689 ± 86 nm in collagen); spinning disk confocal images of phalloidin-stained actin (505 ± 49 nm for a sheet and 533 ± 123 nm for a rosette petal); and scanning electron micrographs, which suggest a thickness of ~640 nm (Fleck et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from confocal microscopy of fixed, phalloidin-stained cells.

claim: Scanning electron micrographs suggest a pseudopod thickness of ~640 nm.
source: The thickness measured from surface-rendered LLSm data agrees with measurements made on other types of data, including: raw lattice light sheet data (567 ± 64 nm on glass and 689 ± 86 nm in collagen); spinning disk confocal images of phalloidin-stained actin (505 ± 49 nm for a sheet and 533 ± 123 nm for a rosette petal); and scanning electron micrographs, which suggest a thickness of ~640 nm (Fleck et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from scanning electron micrographs, with citation to Fleck et al., 2005.

claim: Lamellar pseudopods are not perfectly flat, and exhibit varying degrees of pucker and undulation.
source: Lamellar pseudopods are not perfectly flat, and exhibit varying degrees of pucker and undulation.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from three-dimensional imaging of pseudopod morphology.

claim: In uniform fields of chemoattractant, both lamellar and rosette pseudopods are highly dynamic and ephemeral.
source: In uniform fields of chemoattractant, both lamellar and rosette pseudopods are highly dynamic and ephemeral (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on observations from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Ambient occlusion tonal surface rendering makes cellular structures more easily interpretable by emphasizing the spatial relationships of three-dimensional surfaces and variations in surface texture.
source: Tonal surface rendering with ambient occlusion makes cellular structures more easily interpretable by emphasizing the spatial relationships of three-dimensional surfaces and variations in surface texture.
evidence: The claim describes the benefits of the ambient occlusion rendering technique used in the study.

claim: The enhanced ability to detect and interpret textures and protrusions can be seen by comparing traditional maximum intensity projection and rendered versions of confocal data.
source: The enhanced ability to detect and interpret textures and protrusions can be seen by comparing traditional maximum intensity projection and rendered versions of confocal data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and similar renderings of the lattice light sheet data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual comparisons shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: HL-60 cells produce two distinctive types of dynamic membrane protrusion at the leading edge: thin, sheet-like lamina and 'rosettes' formed by the coincidence of multiple lamina.
source: Using these visualization tools, we observed two distinctive types of dynamic membrane protrusion at the leading edge of HL-60 cells crawling on fibronectin-coated coverslips: (i) thin, sheet-like lamina (Figure 2 and Videos 1–6), and (ii) 'rosettes' formed by the coincidence of multiple lamina (Figure 3, Videos 7–10).
evidence: The claim is based on observations from lattice light sheet microscopy shown in Figures 2 and 3 and associated videos.

claim: The morphology of lamellar and rosette protrusions differ from the spherical blebs produced when the plasma membrane detaches from the underlying cortex.
source: The morphology of these protrusions differ from the spherical blebs produced when the plasma membrane detaches from the underlying cortex (Charras and Paluch, 2008), instead they resemble membrane movements driven by rapid assembly of filamentous actin.
evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations and comparison to known characteristics of blebs, with citation to Charras and Paluch, 2008.

claim: Leading-edge sheets and rosettes are filled with dense actin networks.
source: Using confocal microscopy of fixed cells labeled with phalloidin, we verified that leading-edge sheets and rosettes are filled with dense actin networks (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data of phalloidin-stained cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dynamic sheets and rosettes are readily apparent in surface renderings of three-dimensional lattice light sheet microscopy data, but are not easily identified in two-dimensional projections.
source: Dynamic sheets and rosettes are readily apparent in surface renderings of three-dimensional lattice light sheet microscopy data, but are not easily identified in two-dimensional projections (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2), consistent with the failure of conventional light microscopy to identify these structures.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparisons shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2 demonstrating the advantage of 3D rendering.

claim: Similar lamellar protrusions were observed in fixed Jurkat T cells using scanning electron microscopy.
source: Using scanning electron microscopy, we observed similar lamellar protrusions in fixed Jurkat T cells, another amoeboid cell type that employs fast, low-adhesion crawling through complex environments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by scanning electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Pseudopodial sheets sometimes travel across the dorsal surface of the cell, from front to back or side to side.
source: Lamellar pseudopods were not limited to the plane of the coverslip and, in three-dimensional movies, we observed many pseudopodial sheets travelling across the dorsal surface of the cell, from front to back (Figure 2A and Video 1) or side to side (Video 2).
evidence: The claim is based on observations from time-lapse lattice light sheet microscopy shown in Figure 2A and Videos 1-2.

claim: Most pseudopodial sheets emerged from the cell body and projected directly into the liquid medium without ever contacting the surface of the coverslip.
source: Importantly, most pseudopodial sheets emerged from the cell body and projected directly into the liquid medium without ever contacting the surface of the coverslip (Videos 3 and 4 and time overlay in Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on observations from time-lapse imaging shown in Videos 3 and 4 and Figure 2A.
